stem: In regression, the word 'linear' in 'linear model' refers to linearity in...

options.text: the parameters (the β coefficients)
the predictors: every X must enter as a plain straight-line term
the response variable Y, which must be normally distributed
the residuals, which must lie on a straight line

explanation: A model is linear if it is linear in the β's. X², log(X), etc. are fine: they are just new predictors.

stem: Which of these models is NOT linear in the sense needed for OLS?

options.text: Sales = β0 · exp(β1 · TV) + ε
Sales = β0 + β1·TV + β2·TV² + ε
log(Sales) = β0 + β1·log(TV) + ε
Sales = β0 + β1·TV + ε

explanation: β0·exp(β1·TV) is non-linear in the parameters. The quadratic and log-log models are still linear in β.

stem: You fit mpg = β0 + β1·hp + β2·hp² + ε. A colleague says: 'You can't use OLS, that's a nonlinear model.' What is the best response?

options.text: OLS still applies: the model is linear in β with hp² as just another predictor, even though the fitted curve bends in hp
The colleague is right: a squared term requires nonlinear least squares instead of OLS
OLS applies only if hp and hp² are uncorrelated
OLS applies, but t-tests on the coefficients are no longer valid

explanation: Polynomial regression is still a linear combination of predictors, so it is a linear model and OLS works as usual.

stem: Testing H0: β1 = 0 vs Ha: β1 ≠ 0, you reject H0 at the 5% level. This tells you...

options.text: there is statistically significant evidence that β1 is not zero
the effect of X on Y is large enough to matter in practice
X causes Y
the model's R² is above 0.05

explanation: Rejecting H0 means the estimate is far enough from zero (relative to its SE) that zero is implausible. It says nothing about size or causation.

stem: Two predictors of weekly sales: TV budget has β̂ = 0.047 (p < 0.0001); store size has β̂ = 3.5 (p = 0.20). Which statement is supported?

options.text: There is strong evidence TV has a non-zero effect; the store-size estimate is too imprecise to rule out zero
TV has the larger effect on sales because its p-value is much smaller
Store size is more strongly related to sales because its coefficient is larger
Both are significant because both coefficients are positive

explanation: p-values measure evidence against β = 0, not effect size. Coefficient size depends on units, so neither comparison says which effect is bigger.

stem: With data on 1,000,000 customers, a coupon's coefficient is 0.002 extra units sold (p < 0.001). The manager says: 'Highly significant, so this is our most important lever.' What is the flaw?

options.text: With a huge sample even a tiny effect is significant; 0.002 units may be practically negligible
There is no flaw: a p-value below 0.001 indicates a very large effect
The p-value must be wrong, because large samples make p-values larger
The coefficient should be compared to R² before calling it significant

explanation: Significance tells you the effect is not zero. With n = 1,000,000 the standard error is tiny, so even a trivial effect is significant.

stem: In simple linear regression, which quantity measures how strongly (how tightly) X and Y are linearly related?

options.text: R², which equals r² when there is one predictor
The slope β̂1: a bigger slope means a stronger relationship
The intercept β̂0
The residual sum of squares, RSS

explanation: R² is the share of variance in Y explained by X. The slope's size depends on the units of X and Y.

stem: Regressing Sales on TV budget in dollars gives β̂1 = 0.000047. Re-measuring TV budget in thousands of dollars gives β̂1 = 0.047. What happened to R²?

options.text: Nothing: R² is unchanged, only the units of the slope changed
It rose: the relationship became 1000 times stronger
It fell by a factor of 1000
It cannot be known without re-running the t-test

explanation: Rescaling X rescales the slope but leaves the fit (RSS, TSS, R²) identical.

stem: Two simple regressions predict the same Y. Predictor A: β̂1 = 5.0, R² = 0.10. Predictor B: β̂1 = 0.5, R² = 0.85. Which predictor gives more accurate predictions of Y?

options.text: B: it explains 85% of the variance in Y; slope size depends on units and says nothing about fit
A: its slope is 10 times larger, so it is more strongly related to Y
They are equivalent because both slopes are positive
You need the p-values, because the smaller p-value marks the stronger predictor

explanation: Prediction accuracy is about how much variance is explained (R²), not how steep the line is.

stem: In Sales = β0 + β1·TV + β2·Radio + β3·Newspaper + ε, the coefficient β2 means...

options.text: the change in Sales for a one-unit increase in Radio, holding TV and Newspaper fixed
the total change in Sales associated with Radio, including the TV and Newspaper spending that usually moves with it
the share of Sales explained by Radio
the correlation between Radio and Sales

explanation: Each coefficient in a multiple regression is the effect of that predictor with all other predictors held fixed.

stem: A simple regression of Sales on Newspaper gives β̂ = 0.055 (significant). In the multiple regression with TV and Radio, Newspaper's β̂ ≈ -0.001 (not significant). Most likely explanation?

options.text: Newspaper spending is correlated with Radio; once Radio is held fixed, Newspaper adds no extra information
One of the regressions must be wrong: the same variable should get the same coefficient in both
Collinearity between Newspaper and Radio biased the multiple-regression estimate toward zero
Newspaper advertising has a negative effect on sales

explanation: The simple regression picks up Radio's effect through Newspaper (they are correlated). Holding Radio fixed removes it.

stem: A sales model includes price and a promotion dummy; promotions usually run together with price cuts. The manager asks: 'What happens if we run a promotion WITHOUT changing price?' Which estimate answers this?

options.text: The promotion coefficient from the multiple regression that also includes price
The coefficient from a simple regression of sales on promotion alone, because it captures the full promotion effect
Neither: promotion and price are correlated, so the multiple-regression coefficients are biased and cannot answer it
The price coefficient, because promotions work through price

explanation: 'Promotion with price unchanged' is exactly 'holding price fixed', which is what the multiple-regression coefficient measures. The simple regression mixes in the price cuts.

stem: What is the main consequence of collinearity (highly correlated predictors) in a regression?

options.text: Larger standard errors: coefficient estimates become noisy and imprecise
Biased coefficient estimates that are systematically too high or too low
A sharp drop in R²
Heteroscedastic residuals

explanation: Collinearity inflates Var(β̂) (see VIF). Estimates stay unbiased but become noisy.

stem: Balance is regressed on rating and credit limit, which are almost perfectly correlated. The SE of limit's coefficient is 12 times larger than in a model with age and limit, and limit is no longer significant. What should you conclude?

options.text: Limit's estimate is now very imprecise; its insignificance may reflect collinearity rather than no effect
Limit's coefficient is now biased, so the model with rating is invalid
Limit has no effect on balance
The effect of limit now includes the effect of rating

explanation: Collinearity makes it hard to separate the two effects, so SEs balloon. That can hide a real effect without biasing it.

stem: Which is the more serious problem: (a) leaving out a variable correlated with both Y and another predictor, or (b) including two highly correlated predictors?

options.text: (a): omitted-variable bias makes estimates systematically wrong, while collinearity only makes them noisy
(b): collinearity biases every coefficient, while omitting a variable just lowers R²
They are equally serious because both violate corr(X, ε) = 0
Neither affects coefficient estimates; they only affect R²

explanation: Lecture 4: omitted-variable bias 'creates more problem', since it biases estimates. Collinearity leads to noisy estimates.

stem: Income = β0 + β1·Female + ε, where Female = 1 for women and 0 for men. β̂1 estimates...

options.text: mean income of women minus mean income of men
mean income of women
mean income of men
the probability that a person is female

explanation: β̂0 is the base group's (men's) mean; β̂1 is the difference between women and the base.

stem: Spending = β0 + β1·Summer + β2·Fall + β3·Winter + ε, with Spring as the base season. Estimates: β̂0 = 200, β̂2 = 30. Estimated average spending in Fall is...
explanation: Fall's mean = base (Spring) mean + Fall's difference = 200 + 30 = 230.

stem: Same seasonal model with Spring as base: β̂0 = 200, β̂Summer = 50, β̂Fall = 30, β̂Winter = -20. Which season has the highest estimated average spending?

options.text: Summer, at 250
Spring, at 200, since it has the largest coefficient
Summer, at 50
It cannot be determined without a model that uses Summer as the base

explanation: Season means: Spring 200, Summer 250, Fall 230, Winter 180. Each dummy is a difference from Spring.

stem: Adding one more predictor to an OLS regression will always...

options.text: keep R² the same or raise it on the training data, even if the predictor is useless, without guaranteeing better predictions
improve the model's predictions on new data
raise the test MSE
lower R² if the predictor is useless

explanation: Training RSS can only go down as predictors are added. That is why RSS/R² cannot be used to choose among models of different sizes.

stem: Polynomial fits of degree 1, 2 and 5 have training MSE 24, 19, 15 and test MSE 25, 20, 27. Which degree should you choose?

options.text: Degree 2: lowest test MSE
Degree 5: lowest training MSE
Degree 1: a straight line has both the lowest bias and the lowest variance
None can be chosen without R²

explanation: We care about new data, so compare test MSE. Smallest training MSE ≠ smallest test MSE.

stem: A model has R² = 0.99 on training data but much larger error on a holdout set. Best diagnosis and fix?

options.text: Overfitting: it is fitting noise; reduce flexibility or regularize, and choose complexity by validation error
The model is excellent; the holdout set must be unrepresentative, so report the training R²
High bias: add more polynomial terms to make it more flexible
Heteroscedasticity: use robust standard errors

explanation: A big gap between training and test error is the signature of overfitting (high variance).

stem: As a model becomes more flexible (e.g., a higher polynomial degree), typically...

options.text: bias decreases and variance increases
bias increases and variance decreases
both bias and variance decrease
both bias and variance increase

explanation: Flexible models can follow the true shape (low bias) but change a lot between training sets (high variance).

stem: A straight line is fitted to data that clearly curve. The prediction error is mainly due to...

options.text: high bias: the model is too simple to capture the true shape
high variance: a straight line changes a lot from one training sample to the next
irreducible error Var(ε), which no model can remove
overfitting to noise in the training data

explanation: Bias is the error from approximating a complicated truth with a too-simple f(). A straight line on curved data underfits.

stem: You refit a degree-10 polynomial on many different training samples. The fitted curves vary wildly, but on average they track the true curve. What does this show, and what would help?

options.text: High variance, low bias: reduce flexibility, regularize, or add data
High bias: raise the degree further so each fit matches its sample better
Irreducible error: nothing can reduce it
Nothing is wrong as long as each fit has low training MSE

explanation: Var(f̂) measures how much f̂ changes across training sets. Tracking the truth on average means low bias.

stem: Why do we hold out a validation set instead of just measuring error on the training data?

options.text: Error on the data the model was fitted to is overly optimistic; we need data the model has not seen
It is not really needed: if n is large, training error is a fine estimate of prediction error
To have more data for estimating the coefficients
To make R² higher

explanation: The fit minimizes training error, so MSE_train < MSE_test. Only unseen data measures out-of-sample performance.

stem: In 5-fold cross-validation, each observation is...

options.text: used for validation exactly once, and for training in the other 4 fits
used for both training and validation within the same fit, and the errors are averaged
used only for training; validation uses a separate fresh dataset
used in only one of the 5 fits

explanation: Each fold takes a turn as the validation set while the model is fit on the other k-1 folds.

stem: An analyst tries 50 values of λ, picks the one with the lowest error on the test set, and reports that test error as the model's expected performance. What is the problem?

options.text: The test set was used for tuning, so its error is optimistic; tune with cross-validation and keep the test set for the final estimate
No problem: the test set was not used to estimate coefficients, so its error is unbiased
λ should have been tuned on training error, which is more stable
The only problem is that 50 values of λ is too few

explanation: Choosing λ by test error makes the test set part of model selection, so the reported error is biased downward.

stem: Ridge regression minimizes RSS + λ·Σβj². As λ becomes very large, the coefficient estimates...

options.text: shrink toward zero
approach the OLS estimates
all become exactly zero at some finite λ
grow larger in magnitude

explanation: A large λ makes the penalty dominate, pulling all β's toward 0. λ = 0 gives OLS.

stem: Which value of λ gives the most flexible ridge model (lowest bias, highest variance)?

options.text: λ = 0, which is just OLS
All values are equally flexible because the same predictors are used

explanation: More λ means more shrinkage, so less flexibility. λ = 0 applies no penalty at all.

stem: Cross-validated error vs λ for ridge is U-shaped: high at very small λ, lowest at λ = 5, high again at very large λ. How do you explain the two ends?

options.text: Small λ: little shrinkage, high variance (overfitting). Large λ: heavy shrinkage, high bias (underfitting).
Small λ: heavy shrinkage, underfitting. Large λ: close to OLS, overfitting.
Small λ: little shrinkage, which causes high bias. Large λ: heavy shrinkage, which causes high variance.
Both ends overfit; only the middle avoids it

explanation: λ controls flexibility: small λ ≈ OLS with all predictors (variance), large λ ≈ all β's near 0 (bias).

stem: Which method can set some coefficients exactly to zero, performing variable selection?

options.text: LASSO
Both ridge regression and LASSO
Ordinary least squares
Neither: only best subset selection can

explanation: LASSO's L1 penalty produces exact zeros; ridge shrinks toward zero but never exactly to it.

stem: You have 200 predictors and want an interpretable model that uses only a handful of them. Which shrinkage method fits this goal?

options.text: LASSO, because its L1 penalty can set many coefficients exactly to zero
Ridge, because it shrinks unimportant coefficients to exactly zero
Ridge with λ = 0, which gives the strongest selection
OLS with all 200 predictors

explanation: Only LASSO does automatic variable selection. Ridge keeps all 200 predictors, just shrunk.

stem: Why does LASSO produce coefficients that are exactly zero while ridge does not?

options.text: LASSO's constraint region |β1| + |β2| ≤ s has corners on the axes, where the RSS contours tend to touch it; ridge's circle has no corners
Both give exact zeros for large enough λ; LASSO just reaches them at a smaller λ
Ridge requires standardized predictors, which prevents zeros
LASSO uses a squared penalty, which grows faster near zero

explanation: Geometrically, the OLS ellipse first touches the diamond at a corner (a zero coefficient); a circle is touched at a generic point.

stem: Before fitting ridge or LASSO, predictors should usually be...

options.text: standardized, so each has standard deviation 1
left in their original units, since shrinkage methods are scale invariant like OLS
log-transformed
converted into dummy variables

explanation: The penalty treats all β's alike, so predictors must be on a common scale. OLS is scale invariant; ridge/LASSO are not.

stem: In a ridge regression without standardization, you re-measure income from dollars to thousands of dollars. What happens?

options.text: The fit changes: income's coefficient is penalized differently, which also changes the other coefficients
Nothing changes except that income's coefficient scales by 1000, exactly as in OLS
Income drops out of the model
The penalty λ is automatically rescaled, so the fit is identical

explanation: Lecture 5: ridge coefficients are not scale invariant, and the fit of one coefficient depends on the scale of the others.

stem: Age (years, SD 10) and income (dollars, SD 20,000) are both truly important. You fit LASSO WITHOUT standardizing. What is likely?

options.text: Age's per-unit coefficient is large, so it is penalized far more heavily and may be dropped unfairly
Both are treated fairly because LASSO, like OLS, does not depend on units
Neither is dropped, because only ridge drops variables
Income is dropped because its raw values are larger

explanation: A per-dollar coefficient is tiny, so its penalty is tiny; a per-year coefficient is big and gets shrunk hard. Standardizing fixes this.

stem: In the logistic model ln(P / (1 - P)) = β0 + β1·X, β1 is the change in ___ for a one-unit increase in X.

options.text: the log-odds that Y = 1
the probability that Y = 1
the value of Y
the odds that Y = 1, added directly to the current odds

explanation: The logit model is linear in the log-odds. The effect on odds is multiplicative (× e^β1), and the effect on probability varies.

stem: In the Coke-vs-Pepsi logit model, price_Coke has β̂ = -0.9665 (odds ratio 0.380). What does a $1 increase in Coke's price do?

options.text: Multiplies the odds of buying Coke by about 0.38 (a 62% drop in the odds)
Lowers the probability of buying Coke by 0.9665
Lowers the probability of buying Coke by 62 percentage points
Makes the probability of buying Coke equal to 0.38

explanation: exp(-0.9665) = 0.380 is an odds ratio. It scales the odds; it is not a probability or a change in probability.

stem: The linear probability model gives price_Coke = -0.129; the logit gives -0.9665. A classmate says the logit shows a price effect 7 times larger. Best response?

options.text: The numbers aren't comparable: -0.129 is a change in probability, -0.9665 a change in log-odds, whose effect on probability depends on the baseline
Agreed: both are changes in purchase probability and the logit's is bigger
They should be equal, since a price change shifts probability by the same amount for every customer; one model is misspecified
The LPM coefficient is in odds, so exponentiate it before comparing

explanation: LPM coefficients are probability changes; logit coefficients are log-odds changes. They live on different scales.

stem: If the probability of an event is 0.2, its odds are...
The odds that a customer buys are 1 : 3. What is the probability that the customer buys?

options.text: 0.33 (one third)

explanation: Odds m : n means probability m / (m + n) = 1 / 4.

stem: An in-store display has an odds ratio of 2 for purchase. For a customer whose purchase probability was 0.5, what does the display do?

options.text: Doubles the odds from 1 to 2, so the probability rises to about 0.67
Doubles the probability, from 0.5 to 1.0
Raises the probability by 2 percentage points, to 0.52
Doubles the log-odds

explanation: P = 0.5 means odds = 1. Doubling gives odds 2, i.e., P = 2/3.

stem: In a logit model the marginal effect of Xj on P(Y = 1) is βj · P · (1 - P). When is this effect largest?

options.text: When P is close to 0.5
It is the same for everyone: it always equals βj
When P is close to 0 or 1
When Xj equals zero

explanation: P·(1 - P) peaks at P = 0.5 (value 0.25) and shrinks toward 0 near P = 0 or 1.

stem: Coke loyalists have P(Coke) ≈ 0.95; switchers have P(Coke) ≈ 0.5. In a logit model, a rise in Pepsi's price changes P(Coke) the most for...

options.text: switchers
both groups equally, because the price coefficient is the same for everyone
loyalists, because they are more likely to buy Coke anyway
neither: price changes only affect the odds, not the probability

explanation: The marginal effect β·P·(1 - P) is about 0.25β for switchers and about 0.05β for loyalists.

stem: Using a logit model, you want to send a coupon to the customers whose purchase probability it will change the most. Whom should you target?

options.text: Customers with predicted probability near 0.5, where βP(1 - P) is largest
Anyone: the coupon's coefficient implies the same probability boost for every customer
Customers with the highest predicted probability, since they respond most
Customers for whom the coefficient is largest, since β is the probability boost

explanation: Customers who are nearly certain either way (P ≈ 0 or 1) barely move; the 'switchers' near 0.5 move most.

stem: Sensitivity is...

options.text: TP / (TP + FN): the share of actual positives correctly classified
TN / (TN + FP): the share of actual negatives correctly classified
(TP + TN) / total: the share of all cases correctly classified
TP / (TP + FP): the share of predicted positives that are correct

explanation: Sensitivity = true positive rate. Specificity = true negative rate.

stem: There are 100 fraud cases and 9,900 legitimate ones. The model flags 80 of the fraud cases and 99 of the legitimate ones. What is its sensitivity?
explanation: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / 100. Specificity = 9,801 / 9,900 = 99%. Accuracy = 98.8%.

stem: In fraud detection, a missed fraud (false negative) costs the bank far more than a false alarm. Which measure should the bank prioritize?

options.text: Sensitivity: catch as many actual frauds as possible, accepting more false alarms
Specificity, because it measures how many fraud cases are caught
Total accuracy, because it combines both error types
R² of the logit model

explanation: False negatives reduce sensitivity. When FNs are costly, you push sensitivity up.

stem: If you raise the classification threshold (e.g., from 0.5 to 0.9), sensitivity...

options.text: decreases
increases
stays the same, because the model has not changed
becomes equal to specificity

explanation: A higher threshold labels fewer cases positive, so fewer actual positives are caught.

stem: Raising the threshold from 0.55 to 0.9 will typically...

options.text: reduce false positives and increase false negatives
increase false positives and reduce false negatives
reduce both false positives and false negatives
increase both false positives and false negatives

explanation: Fewer cases are called positive, so fewer false alarms, but more real positives are missed.

stem: A bank wants fewer missed frauds and will accept more false alarms. How should it move the threshold, and what happens to specificity?

options.text: Lower the threshold; sensitivity rises and specificity falls
Raise the threshold; sensitivity rises and specificity falls
Lower the threshold; specificity rises because more fraud is caught
Keep it at 0.5; the threshold does not affect which frauds are caught

explanation: Lower threshold means more positives flagged: sensitivity up, specificity down.

stem: Only 2% of transactions are fraud. A 'model' that labels every transaction as not-fraud has 98% accuracy. What does this show?

options.text: Accuracy is misleading for rare events: this model catches zero fraud
It is a strong model, since 98% accuracy is very high
Its specificity is 0%
The accuracy must have been computed incorrectly

explanation: Sensitivity is 0% (no fraud caught) even though accuracy is 98%; the majority class dominates accuracy.

stem: Fraud is 2% of cases and missed fraud is costly. Model A: 98.5% accuracy, 10% sensitivity. Model B: 93% accuracy, 85% sensitivity. Which do you choose?

options.text: B: it catches most fraud; A's accuracy mostly reflects the 98% non-fraud cases
A: higher overall accuracy means better classification
A: 10% sensitivity means only 10% false alarms
They are equivalent

explanation: A misses 90% of fraud. With rare, costly events, sensitivity matters far more than raw accuracy.

stem: After oversampling fraud cases to 20% of the training data, accuracy drops from 98% to 90% but sensitivity rises from 5% to 70%. A teammate says oversampling made the model worse. Response?

options.text: Disagree: the 98% came from predicting the majority class; the model now actually detects fraud
Agree: accuracy fell by 8 points, so the model got worse
Agree: higher sensitivity means more false alarms, so the model is worse
They cannot be compared, because oversampling changes the coefficients

explanation: With rare events, a jump from 5% to 70% sensitivity is a big improvement even though accuracy drops.
